title_original: Art Mania by Kitty Hauser review – the gripping story of the man behind the Western Desert art movement
excerpt_original: Biography of Geoffrey Bardon breaks new ground in the story of contemporary Aboriginal art and the billion-dollar market that sprung up around it Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email In 1971, Geoffrey Bardon, a 30-year-old school teacher and artist from Sydney, arrived at…

blocks.text: I n 1971, Geoffrey Bardon, a 30-year-old school teacher and artist from Sydney, arrived at the remote Northern Territory Aboriginal settlement of Papunya, on Pintupi country, to take up a position at the government-run school.

Over the next 18 months, he set up a painting centre for the Aboriginal men, encouraging them to transpose ceremonial designs – traditionally inscribed on the sand or body – on to boards, and started selling the artworks on their behalf.

What occurred under his purview is generally heralded as the origin point of contemporary Aboriginal art, and the nationwide art centre system and multibillion dollar international market that sprung up around it.

There were, of course, already Aboriginal people making art – most famously, Albert Namatjira and the Hermannsburg painters. But the Papunya movement spearheaded the aesthetic of dots, concentric circles and lines that most international and non-Indigenous Australian audiences associate with Aboriginal art.

Like all cultural myths, this story bears close scrutiny – and Kitty Hauser’s Art Mania: Geoffrey Bardon and the Painting Men of Papunya is only the latest in a line of academic and journalistic investigations of the Papunya story.

Hauser focuses on Bardon – specifically his mental health and personal history, and how it influenced the reality and myth of Papunya. She breaks new ground by identifying the key role his brother Jim, an aspiring author, played in shaping the stories of both Geoff and Papunya art.

The subject matter is important, because Bardon became one of the key arbiters of Papunya art and the broader movement that arose around it, known as Western Desert art – often to the exclusion of the artists themselves.

blocks.text: Though the Bardon mythology has been interrogated and partially debunked in the decades since, aspects have proved persistent, including the significance of the paintings, how they are read, and the idea that they represent a uniquely “authentic” kind of Aboriginal art.

Hauser weaves a fascinating and gripping tale, partly because it is cast as a mystery, about something that happened to Bardon at Papunya that dramatically shaped his life thereafter and the stories he told about the painting men and their art.

Bardon and his brother were scions of a once-important family in Sydney’s Randwick, who grew up in a fairly unhappy home. Both had artistic ambitions – Geoff as a film-maker and Jim as an author – though each followed more traditional career paths (Jim was a solicitor).

Drawing on Geoff’s personal archives, his unpublished biography co-written with Jim, and conversations with friends, family and colleagues, Hauser paints a picture of someone who was in some ways well suited to the work he would undertake at Papunya: diffident, affable, generous, curious and enthusiastic. Someone who yearned to contribute something of importance to Australian culture.

Geoff saw his Papunya assignment as a romantic adventure and grist for his artistic mill. But the settlement was a shock to his system: a surreal and alienating environment for someone raised in white suburbia – from the regimented living arrangements and culture of the “welfare” apparatus, to the desert landscape and climate. It was also his first substantial encounter with Aboriginal people and culture, living in proximity to Pintupi, Luritja, Warlpiri, Anmatyerr, Kukatja and Arrernte people.

He was immediately struck by the gravitas of the men he encountered – including now-famous figures such as Tim Leura Tjapaltjarri and Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri – and their ceremonies, stories and designs. He became wholly absorbed with the heroic notion of fostering a new strain of Aboriginal art.

Working outside his job remit, Bardon set up an ad hoc studio for the men, bought materials with his own money, taught them how to work with different kinds of paint, and gave them feedback on composition. He also started promoting and selling the art, establishing a valuable source of revenue for the artists and their communities.

Geoff’s arrival at Papunya seems to have coincided with a manic phase in his mental health, characterised by preternatural energy, excitement and grandiosity. It fuelled the painting project but was unsustainable and blossomed into insecurity and paranoia – about the settlement’s administrators, his colleagues and local art contacts.

And then came the crash: in 1972 Geoff suffered a nervous breakdown, and Jim had to travel to Papunya to bring him back to Sydney. In the aftermath, he was admitted to a private psychiatric hospital, where he underwent a controversial – and subsequently notorious – treatment called Deep Sleep Therapy , that inflicted lasting psychological damage.

The mania, breakdown and trauma of treatment profoundly shaped how Bardon told the story of Papunya. His diminished capacity also left the path open for Jim, who had his own baggage and ambitions, to take the lead role in Geoff’s various writings about the movement. Between them, they spun a mythology with Geoff at the centre, as a kind of tragic hero; a white saviour and truthteller who martyred himself for Aboriginal art. A narrative that eclipsed the agency of the painting men.

Hauser’s overarching thesis maps Geoff’s experience on to that of white Australia, and it’s true that many aspects of his story are emblematic of a kind of grander narrative of white narcissism and paternalism towards the continent’s First Peoples.
Art Mania also paints a troubling picture of how ignorant many of the people who were promulgating – and often profiting from – Aboriginal art were about the cultures underpinning it.
But Hauser’s book is most convincing and powerful as a cautionary tale: about who gets to tell stories – and the immense amount of personal baggage they bring to the telling.
Art Mania: Geoffrey Bardon and the Painting Men of Papunya by Kitty Hauser is available now (Giramondo; $39.95)
